list-item.p: Zanubrutinib demonstrated significantly longer PFS vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax (HR = 0.45, P = .0197) in treatment-naïve fit patients with CLL.
The robustness of these results was supported by matching-adjusted indirect comparison analyses.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In the phase 3 randomized SEQUOIA study (NCT03336333), zanubrutinib (arm A) demonstrated superior progression-free survival (PFS) compared with bendamustine-rituximab (BR; arm B) in patients with treatment-naive chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) without del(17p). In the phase 3 AMPLIFY study (NCT03836261), acalabrutinib-venetoclax with or without obinutuzumab demonstrated prolonged PFS vs chemoimmunotherapy (investigator’s choice of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab [FCR] or BR) in patients with treatment-naive CLL without del(17p) or TP53 mutations. Compared with AMPLIFY, the patient population in SEQUOIA was unsuitable for FCR and included patients with TP53 mutations. The aim of this post hoc analysis was to investigate the efficacy of zanubrutinib in patients from SEQUOIA vs a clinically similar patient population treated with acalabrutinib-venetoclax in AMPLIFY. A numerically greater 3-year investigator-assessed PFS (PFS-INV) was observed with zanubrutinib (84.3%) in the SEQUOIA population vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax in AMPLIFY (78.9%). When matching SEQUOIA to the AMPLIFY population by FCR eligibility, a greater PFS benefit with zanubrutinib was reported (89.2% vs 78.9%, respectively). To support the comparison of zanubrutinib vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax, an anchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison was performed, which showed that zanubrutinib was associated with prolonged PFS-INV vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax when adjusted for various baseline characteristics. Zanubrutinib also demonstrated longer PFS whether adjusted for age (PFS-INV hazard ratio [HR], 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.13-0.54; P < .0003) or unadjusted (PFS-INV HR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.23-0.88; P = .0197). These results highlight zanubrutinib monotherapy as an effective treatment option for all patients with treatment-naive CLL/SLL, including patients who might otherwise be considered for more intensive fixed-duration combination regimens.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The development of medications that target B-cell receptor signaling in chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) has revolutionized the treatment landscape for this disease.1, 2, 3, 4 In the first-line setting, Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor with or without a cluster of differentiation 20 antibody (CD20), fixed-duration B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2) inhibitor in combination with a CD20 antibody, and fixed-duration minimal residual disease–guided BTK inhibitor in combination with a B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor until disease progression have emerged as effective therapies in treatment-naive CLL.4 Understanding which treatment combinations and durations will be most effective in different patient populations is critical in identifying optimal treatment strategies for patients with CLL/SLL. However, head-to-head studies to inform clinicians about which treatment modalities may be most effective for their patients are often lacking.

Zanubrutinib is a highly potent and selective next-generation BTK inhibitor that is approved for treatment-naive and relapsed/refractory CLL/SLL globally, including in the United States and the European Union.5, 6, 7 Zanubrutinib was designed to provide complete and sustained BTK occupancy for efficacy across multiple B-cell malignancies, with fewer off-target adverse events compared with other BTK inhibitors, such as ibrutinib.5,7,8

In the global, open-label, phase 3 SEQUOIA trial, treatment-naive patients with CLL/SLL without del(17p) were randomized to continuous treatment with zanubrutinib until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity (cohort 1, arm A) or 6 cycles of bendamustine-rituximab (BR; cohort 1, arm B). Patients with del(17p) were also enrolled and treated with zanubrutinib (cohort 2, arm C). These patients were not randomly assigned because chemoimmunotherapy was not considered a suitable option based on international guidelines.9,10 In arm A, zanubrutinib demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) vs BR patients in arm B, after a median follow-up of 26.2 months; the 24-month PFS rate was 85.5% and 69.5%, respectively.11 At the 5-year follow-up, median PFS was not met in the zanubrutinib arm and was 44.1 months in the BR arm.12

In SEQUOIA, enrolled patients were aged ≥65 years, or 18 to 64 years with comorbidities, and were thus unsuitable for fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab (FCR).11,12 Understanding the efficacy and tolerability of zanubrutinib in more fit patient populations, defined as treatment-naive patients with CLL/SLL without del(17p) or TP53 mutations who may be suitable for FCR, may help facilitate informed clinical decisions and improve patient outcomes.

Fixed-duration combinations such as ibrutinib plus venetoclax and venetoclax plus obinutuzumab have shown notable success in treatment-naive CLL, prolonging PFS compared with chemoimmunotherapy.13, 14, 15 The global, open-label, phase 3 AMPLIFY study evaluated the efficacy of a fixed-duration BTK inhibitor–based regimen, acalabrutinib-venetoclax with or without obinutuzumab, vs chemoimmunotherapy (investigator’s choice of FCR or BR) in patients with treatment-naive CLL without del(17p) or TP53 mutations.15 At a median follow-up of 40.8 months, the estimated 36-month PFS rate was 76.5% with acalabrutinib-venetoclax, 83.1% with acalabrutinib-venetoclax-obinutuzumab, and 66.5% with FCR or BR.

In contrast to SEQUOIA, the AMPLIFY study enrolled a younger and more fit patient population, only enrolling patients with a Cumulative Illness Rating Scale (CIRS) score of ≤6 and creatinine clearance of ≥50 mL/min for acalabrutinib-venetoclax, acalabrutinib-venetoclax-obinutuzumab, and BR or creatinine clearance of ≥70 mL/min for FCR. Although both zanubrutinib monotherapy (in SEQUOIA) and acalabrutinib-venetoclax (in AMPLIFY) demonstrated prolonged PFS compared with chemoimmunotherapy, no head-to-head trials comparing these treatment options have been conducted.

Outcomes in patients with more fit characteristics in SEQUOIA, who may be candidates for intensive fixed-duration combination treatments, have not been previously examined. In this post hoc analysis, we first investigated the efficacy of zanubrutinib in the fit subgroup of patients with CLL from SEQUOIA (defined as creatinine clearance of ≥50 mL/min, CIRS score of ≤6 and without del(17p)/TP53 mutations) compared with a clinically similar patient population treated with acalabrutinib-venetoclax in AMPLIFY; this was done by applying the relevant AMPLIFY eligibility criteria to the randomized cohort of SEQUOIA for an unadjusted indirect comparison analysis.

To further test the robustness of the unadjusted indirect comparison results in the fit populations in the 2 studies, matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) statistical analyses were also conducted. As differences in patient characteristics in cross-trial comparisons may lead to bias when comparing treatment outcomes, a MAIC analysis was done as it adjusts for differences in patient populations and can be used to compare the efficacy and safety of different treatment regimens when direct comparisons are not available.16 MAIC analyses have been used successfully to compare different regimens across CLL/SLL studies.17,18

sec.title: Methods
sec.p:
The SEQUOIA (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03336333) and AMPLIFY (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03836261) study designs and primary results have been previously reported.11 This post hoc analysis compared zanubrutinib-treated patients from SEQUOIA with acalabrutinib-venetoclax–treated patients from AMPLIFY, using an unadjusted analysis of the fit population and a supporting analysis with the MAIC approach. The unadjusted analysis was conducted using classic censoring to identify the fit population (defined as patients with CLL with creatinine clearance of ≥50 mL/min, CIRS score of ≤6, and without del(17p)/TP53 mutations) which would be comparable to the AMPLIFY study population. The supporting analysis, including an anchored MAIC, was conducted in patients with CLL and without del(17p)/TP53 mutations. The analysis groups from cohort 1 of SEQUOIA (Figure 1) comprise the following:1.
The fit subgroup of patients from cohort 1 of SEQUOIA, established by applying the AMPLIFY eligibility criteria to the population. For this analysis, data sets with similar median follow-ups (SEQUOIA, 43.9 months; AMPLIFY, 41.0 months) were used.2.
Patients who did not meet the fit criteria. These patients were then compared with the SEQUOIA fit subgroup.3.
The MAIC population: In the anchored MAIC, individual patient data from zanubrutinib-treated patients were reweighted to match the key population characteristics of AMPLIFY.Figure 1.
SEQUOIA analyses populations. ITT, intention to treat; zanu, zanubrutinib.

sec.title: Main unadjusted analysis in SEQUOIA fit patient subgroup: zanubrutinib vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax
sec.p: Patients enrolled in SEQUOIA were aged ≥65 years, or 18 to 64 years with comorbidities; met ≥1 indication for treatment per International Workshop on CLL criteria; and were considered unsuitable for treatment with FCR. Exclusion criteria for FCR were age ≥65 years, or <65 years with a CIRS score of >6; creatinine clearance of <70 mL/min; or history of severe infections. To determine the fit subgroup in SEQUOIA, the key inclusion criteria from AMPLIFY were used (supplemental Figure 1).15 Patients from cohort 1 of arms A and B were censored if they had SLL, del(17p), TP53 mutation (or missing information), baseline creatinine clearance <50 mL/min (or missing information), or CIRS score >6; the remaining patients were analyzed as the fit subgroup (supplemental Figure 1); 2 patients with del(17p) were misassigned to arm A and were therefore censored when analyzing the fit patient subgroup in the unadjusted analysis and in the MAIC analyses. Efficacy in the fit subgroup in SEQUOIA vs the overall intention-to-treat (ITT) population and those who did not meet the fit criteria was then assessed.

sec.title: Supporting analysis of MAIC: zanubrutinib vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax
sec.p: MAIC uses individual patient-level data (IPD) from 1 study in conjunction with aggregate-level data from a second study to adjust for differences in baseline characteristics, which produces reweighted estimates for analysis.16 Due to key differences in the inclusion criteria between SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY (supplemental Table 1), the baseline clinical characteristics of patients enrolled in these studies were not similar. An anchored MAIC was conducted between the ITT population in zanubrutinib cohort 1 of SEQUOIA and the acalabrutinib-venetoclax arm of AMPLIFY, using the adjusted population from the BR subgroup of arm B cohort 1 of SEQUOIA and the FCR/BR arm of AMPLIFY as common control arms. The rationale for this assumption was based on the similar efficacy data reported when evaluating the FCR and BR treatment groups separately in AMPLIFY (PFS, 68.9% and 64.5%, respectively; OS, 85.5% and 86.4%).15 Anchored MAIC analyses are recommended over unanchored MAIC models (without a common comparator arm) as they require fewer assumptions and minimize residual bias due to unaccounted-for covariates.19 To further bolster the unadjusted and anchored MAIC results, a sensitivity analysis was conducted using an unanchored MAIC without the FCR/BR control arm. Additional sensitivity analyses were also performed to explore different sets of baseline matching factors to support the robustness of the MAIC base case results (supplemental Table 2).

Baseline characteristics used for matching comprised demographics (sex), genetics (del[11q] and immunoglobulin heavy chain variable status), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, and disease status. Pseudo-IPD investigator-assessed PFS (PFS-INV) curves from AMPLIFY were constructed from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves of published data. Pseudo-IPD PFS-INV curves allowed for reconstruction of PFS curves using pseudo-IPD data when actual IPD were unavailable. Visual analysis of pseudo-IPD Kaplan-Meier curves was performed to validate the accuracy of the digitization.

sec.title: Efficacy and safety outcomes
sec.p: The primary efficacy analysis examined PFS-INV. The hazard ratios (HRs), 95% CIs, and P values for PFS-INV were calculated using a weighted Cox proportional hazards regression model. Other key efficacy outcomes included overall response rate (ORR) and complete response rate (defined as complete response and complete response with incomplete hematologic recovery).

Safety outcomes included treatment-related adverse events. For the safety comparisons between SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY, data from the overall patient population (not the “fit” subgroup) treated with zanubrutinib in SEQUOIA was compared with the acalabrutinib- venetoclax population in AMPLIFY. Exposure-adjusted safety results for zanubrutinib and BR were reported in SEQUOIA (fit population).

Ethics committee approval was not required for this post hoc analysis. The SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY trials were approved by the applicable ethics committees and followed the ethical principles of Good Clinical Practice, International Conference on Harmonization guidelines, and the Declaration of Helsinki. Patients provided written informed consent to participate in both studies.11,15

sec.title: Patient demographics and clinical characteristics in the fit subgroup
sec.p:
Of 479 patients enrolled in SEQUOIA cohort 1 (arms A and B), 252 patients (53%; zanubrutinib, n = 123; BR, n = 129) met the fit subgroup criteria: no diagnosis of SLL, no disease harboring del(17p) or TP53 mutations, low comorbidity burden, and adequate renal function (supplemental Figure 1). Baseline demographics of SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY patients included in this analysis are shown in Table 1. Demographic and clinical variables such as sex and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status were well balanced between the SEQUOIA fit subgroup and AMPLIFY. Median age was 71 years in those receiving zanubrutinib and BR in the SEQUOIA fit subgroup and 61 years in those receiving acalabrutinib-venetoclax and FCR/BR in AMPLIFY. Creatinine clearance of <60 mL/min was reported in 19.5% and 22.5% of zanubrutinib- and BR-treated patients in the SEQUOIA subgroup, respectively, and in 13.1% and 10.3% of acalabrutinib-venetoclax– and FCR/BR–treated patients in the AMPLIFY trial. Rates of unmutated immunoglobulin heavy chain variable region were 51.2% (zanubrutinib) and 51.9% (BR) in the SEQUOIA subgroup and 57.4% (acalabrutinib-venetoclax) and 59.3% (FCR/BR) in AMPLIFY. Bulky disease (≥5 cm) was present in 23.5% and 27.9% of patients in the SEQUOIA subgroup, respectively, and 38.8% and 42.8% of patients in AMPLIFY. Complex karyotype status (≥3 abnormalities) was reported in 8.9% and 11.6% in the SEQUOIA subgroup, respectively, and 15.5% and 14.5% in AMPLIFY.Table 1.

sec.title: Comparison of zanubrutinib vs BR
sec.p: At a median follow-up of 40.3 months (range, 39.4-43.9), median PFS was not reached in the fit subgroup in SEQUOIA. Zanubrutinib demonstrated prolonged PFS compared with BR (HR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.13-0.40; P = .0001). PFS-INV estimates were higher with zanubrutinib vs BR at 36 months (89.2% vs 57.9%, respectively) and 42 months (87.1% vs 50.0%) (supplemental Figure 2). In patients treated with zanubrutinib, PFS estimates in the fit subgroup in SEQUOIA were higher than those in the overall ITT population and patients who did not meet the fit criteria. In zanubrutinib-treated patients, the PFS-INV rates at 36 months in the fit subgroup vs patients who did not meet the fit criteria were 89.2% vs 79.1% without COVID-19 adjustment (supplemental Figure 3) and 91.5% vs 87.1% after COVID-19 adjustment, respectively.

In the SEQUOIA fit subgroup, the investigator-assessed ORR with zanubrutinib vs BR was 97.6% vs 88.4%; the complete response rates (complete response/complete response with incomplete hematologic recovery) were 18.7% vs 24.8%, respectively (Table 2).Table 2.

sec.title: Main analysis: zanubrutinib vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax
sec.p:
After matching SEQUOIA to the AMPLIFY population for fitness and risk factors, a greater PFS benefit with zanubrutinib was consistently reported. The 3-year PFS estimate was greater in zanubrutinib-treated patients (fit population) than patients treated with acalabrutinib-venetoclax in AMPLIFY in both unadjusted (investigator assessed: 89.2% and 78.9%, respectively) and COVID-19–adjusted analyses (investigator assessed, 91.5%; IRC assessed, 78.8% [no investigator-assessed COVID-19–adjusted PFS was reported], respectively; Table 3).Table 3.

sec.p:
After population adjustment, key baseline characteristics were well balanced between the SEQUOIA subgroup and the AMPLIFY population (n = 581), with an effective sample size of 206 (Table 4). Similar results were observed in the population adjusted for age based on patients in SEQUOIA without del(17p) or TP53 mutations and with CLL (not including SLL) (HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.13-0.54; P < .0003) (supplemental Figure 4). Multiple sensitivity analyses supported the results in model scenarios for different matching variables (supplemental Table 3). HR values were similar across almost all sensitivity models; comparable HR values were demonstrated for zanubrutinib vs acalabrutinib-venetoclax regardless of other negative prognostic factors, including patients with del(11q), unmutated immunoglobulin heavy chain variable region, or complex karyotypes (supplemental Table 3). Furthermore, these results were consistent with the unanchored MAIC, without the (FCR/BR) control arm assumption (HR, 0.44; 95% CI: 0.21-0.89; P = .0220) (supplemental Figure 5), including in patients with complex karyotypes. Baseline characteristics for the unanchored MAIC are shown in supplemental Table 4.

sec.title: Safety outcomes
sec.p: In SEQUOIA, most patients in the safety population (zanubrutinib, n = 222 [median exposure, 43.84 months]; BR, n = 222 [median exposure, 5.54 and 5.59 months for bendamustine and rituximab, respectively]) had ≥1 treatment-emergent and posttreatment adverse event (zanubrutinib, n = 116 [95.1%]; BR, n = 119 [97.5%]). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 78 patients (63.9%) treated with zanubrutinib and 102 patients (83.6%) treated with BR. Six treatment-emergent adverse events led to death in each arm. Of these, 4 deaths (2 patients in each arm) were due to infections that were considered related to treatment, including COVID-19 and pneumonia/respiratory failure in the zanubrutinib arm and enterocolitis and sepsis in the BR arm.

After adjustment for duration of exposure, the incidence rates (per 100 person-months) of all-grade and grade ≥3 adverse events of special interest were comparable with zanubrutinib and BR, except for all-grade hemorrhage (zanubrutinib, 2.04; BR, 0.36) and neutropenia (all grades: zanubrutinib, 0.54; BR, 3.77; grade ≥3: zanubrutinib, 0.41; BR, 2.99) (Table 5).Table 5.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of zanubrutinib in a subgroup of SEQUOIA patients who would have been eligible for AMPLIFY (ie, CLL, no del(17p)/TP53 mutations, creatinine clearance ≥50 mL/min, and CIRS score ≤6) and compare these data to those from acalabrutinib-venetoclax–treated patients in the AMPLIFY study. Notably, when matching patients in SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY for fitness and risk factors such as age, creatinine clearance, and CIRS score, a greater PFS benefit was always observed with continuous single-agent zanubrutinib at the 36-month landmark compared with fixed-duration acalabrutinib-venetoclax. Both SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with deaths due to COVID-19 affecting both studies. After COVID-19 adjustment, the 36-month PFS estimate remained greater in zanubrutinib-treated patients in the SEQUOIA fit subgroup compared with acalabrutinib-venetoclax–treated patients in AMPLIFY. These results are further supported by the anchored MAIC, which showed that zanubrutinib was associated with prolonged PFS-INV compared with acalabrutinib-venetoclax when adjusted for baseline characteristics, including models that excluded age (HRPFS-INV, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.23-0.88; P = .0197) and those that adjusted for age (HRPFS-INV, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.13-0.54; P < .0003). Sensitivity analyses controlling for other baseline variables supported the robustness of the PFS-INV results. An unanchored MAIC without the FCR/BR control arm assumption further supported the robustness of the results and showed minimal difference in comparison with the anchored MAIC results.

In the SEQUOIA ITT population (both fit patients and patients who would not qualify for AMPLIFY due to being less fit and having high-risk features), a numerically greater 3-year PFS was observed with zanubrutinib (investigator assessed, 84.3%) than with acalabrutinib-venetoclax in AMPLIFY (investigator assessed, 78.9%; independent review committee assessed, 76.5%).15

Comparing zanubrutinib vs BR in the SEQUOIA fit subgroup, prolonged PFS was demonstrated with zanubrutinib. Additionally, higher response rates were observed in fit patients receiving zanubrutinib vs BR (ORR, 97.6% vs 88.4%, respectively). As expected, among zanubrutinib-treated patients, prolonged PFS was seen in fit patients relative to patients who did not meet the fit criteria.

Overall, safety outcomes were consistent with the previously reported safety profile of zanubrutinib.12 No unexpected safety results were observed with zanubrutinib in this analysis. In SEQUOIA, rates of hematologic adverse events were lower with zanubrutinib vs BR, including neutropenia (0.54 vs 3.77, respectively), anemia (0.16 vs 0.56), and thrombocytopenia (0.21 vs 0.43). Of note, rates of atrial fibrillation/flutter (0.16) and hypertension (0.50) were low with zanubrutinib. Safety outcomes were generally comparable between zanubrutinib and acalabrutinib-venetoclax; however, differences in the study design and relative fitness between SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY complicates comparative analyses.

Trials investigating other fixed-duration regimens in patients with treatment-naive CLL/SLL, such as ibrutinib-venetoclax or venetoclax-obinutuzumab, have reported lower PFS rates in patients with higher-risk factors, such as TP53 mutations.14,20 Therefore, continuous regimens such as zanubrutinib may be more suitable for a wide range of patients, encompassing those with lower- or higher- risk characteristics and fit or less fit patients. The safety data in SEQUOIA demonstrate that zanubrutinib was effective and tolerable in the fit subgroup and are consistent with previous data in the ITT population.11

Head-to-head studies are the gold standard when comparing treatments in clinical trials as they directly assess therapies within a single randomized study, ensuring that patient characteristics, study procedures, and outcome assessments are consistent across treatment arms. The CLL17 trial comparing fixed-duration venetoclax-obinutuzumab or venetoclax-ibrutinib, and continuous ibrutinib in treatment-naive patients with CLL/SLL,21 is an important predicate clinical trial model that may provide insights in comparing continuous vs fixed-duration regimens. Additionally, a head-to-head phase 3 trial (CELESTIAL-TNCLL; NCT06073821),22 is currently evaluating fixed-dose zanubrutinib treatment in combination with the BCL2 inhibitor sonrotoclax in comparison with fixed-duration venetoclax and obinutuzumab in patients with treatment-naive CLL.

However, the rapidly evolving clinical landscape in CLL, characterized by multiple treatment modalities, emerging agents with novel mechanisms of action, novel combination regimens, and both continuous vs fixed-duration strategies renders direct head-to-head comparisons across the expanding therapeutic armamentarium highly impractical. Consequently, clinicians face increasing challenges in effectively evaluating all treatment options that may be available.

In the absence of head-to-head trials, indirect comparisons are becoming increasingly critical in helping clinicians to make evidence-based decisions. All individual approaches to indirect comparisons have potential limitations that may negatively affect any inferences between different treatment options. However, utilizing multiple approaches may reduce these biases and improve the robustness of the results. The current analyses incorporated several models to potentially reduce bias, including an unadjusted naive comparison, an anchored MAIC, and an unanchored MAIC. Although each of these approaches have potential limitations specific to the analytic methodology, the overall consistency of these results may provide confidence to clinicians in evaluating treatment options without the availability of head-to-head studies. A head-to-head phase 3 trial (CELESTIAL-TNCLL; NCT06073821), is currently evaluating fixed-dose zanubrutinib treatment in combination with the B-cell lymphoma inhibitor sonrotoclax in comparison with fixed-duration venetoclax and obinutuzumab in patients with treatment-naive CLL. The results of this head-to-head study will help support and provide greater context for the results of the current indirect analysis and facilitate informed decision-making for managing patients with treatment-naive CLL.

A limitation of this analysis is that comparisons were post hoc and not designed or powered to detect differences between zanubrutinib and acalabrutinib-venetoclax treatment groups or between fit subgroups and patients who did not meet the fit criteria. In addition, this post hoc analysis compared cross-trial data for continuous-treatment and fixed-duration regimens, which have different drug exposure times. One benefit of a fixed-duration regimen may be the lower risk of developing drug resistance compared with continuous therapy.23,24 In addition, treatment-free intervals preserve the potential for effective retreatment, as sensitivity to the treatment modality can often be maintained.24 Progression-free survival (PFS2), defined as the time from randomization to disease progression on second-line therapy, may be a valuable outcome when comparing fixed-duration and continuous regimens as it measures long-term disease control and not just the first remission. However, longer follow-up is needed to evaluate this outcome in this post hoc analysis. Furthermore, the current analysis is subject to inherent MAIC limitations, including differences in trial design, assessments, and length of follow-up, which may also limit the generalizability and interpretation of these results.

Overall, these results demonstrate that continuous treatment with zanubrutinib in treatment-naive fit patients with CLL resulted in prolonged PFS compared with fixed-duration acalabrutinib-venetoclax. This unadjusted indirect comparison analysis between the SEQUOIA and AMPLIFY patient populations was supported by both anchored and the unanchored MAIC results, which utilized multiple sensitivity analyses to control for potential bias.

In conclusion, these results highlight zanubrutinib monotherapy as an effective treatment option for all patients with treatment-naive CLL/SLL, including fit patients who might otherwise be considered for more intensive fixed-duration combination regimens.
